beginner: Borage is a big, easy, bushy herb with fuzzy leaves and beautiful blue, star-shaped flowers. Bees absolutely love it, which is why gardeners plant it near vegetables like tomatoes, squash, and strawberries. The young leaves taste like cucumber, and both the leaves and the blue flowers are edible, though you should eat them only in small amounts. Borage grows fast, sprawls out, so give it room, and it drops seed and comes back on its own year after year. It likes the warm part of the year in most gardens and is killed by frost; in hot, humid places it is grown in the cooler months instead.
seasoned: Borage (Borago officinalis), also called starflower, is a large, fast-growing, frost-tender annual herb in the borage family (Boraginaceae), native to the Mediterranean. It builds a bushy, sprawling plant about 2 to 3 ft tall and 1 to 2 ft wide, clothed in coarse, bristly, gray-green leaves, and carries loose clusters of nodding, star-shaped, sky-blue flowers from late spring into fall. Borage is one of the best bee and pollinator plants a garden can grow, a traditional companion set near tomatoes, squash, and strawberries, and a vigorous self-seeder that naturalizes readily once established. Both the cucumber-flavored young leaves and the blue flowers are edible, used fresh as a garnish and in drinks and salads, though borage is best eaten in moderation. It grows through the warm months in cool and temperate regions and is killed by hard frost; in hot, humid climates it is grown instead as a cool-season plant.

beginner: Borage is not fussy about soil and grows well even in poor ground, as long as water drains away and does not pool. Ordinary, well-drained garden soil is perfect. Very rich soil just makes big floppy plants, and soggy soil rots the roots, so pick a spot that drains well and go easy on the compost.
seasoned: Borage is highly adaptable and grows in almost any soil, including poor and sandy ground, provided drainage is adequate; extension descriptions list it as tolerating clay, loam, and sand and even nutritionally poor soil. It is a light feeder, so overly rich soil pushes soft, floppy, leafy growth at the expense of sturdiness and bloom, and constantly wet, poorly drained soil rots its roots. Well-drained soil of moderate to low fertility gives the best-structured plants.

beginner: Borage is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range of about 6.0 to 7.0 is ideal, and it tolerates soil well outside that, so you usually do not need to change anything.
seasoned: Borage performs best across roughly 6.0 to 7.0 and is broadly adaptable to soil chemistry; extension descriptions record it growing in acid, neutral, and alkaline soils alike (tolerating roughly 5.5 to 8.0). pH adjustment is rarely warranted, so focus on drainage and modest fertility instead.

beginner: Plant borage seeds right where you want it to grow, since it does not like being moved. Sow after your last frost in most gardens, or in the cool season where summers are hot. Cover the seeds about half an inch deep; they sprout in a week or two and flower in about eight weeks. Give each plant plenty of room because it gets big and sprawly, keep it in sun, and do not over-fertilize. Snip off faded flowers for more blooms, let a few go to seed so it comes back, and wear gloves because the stems are prickly.
seasoned: Grow borage like a big, easygoing warm-season herb: direct-sow it where it is to grow, because it has a taproot and does not transplant well. Sow after the last spring frost in cool and temperate regions, or in fall and the cool season in hot, humid ones, covering the seed about 1/2 in. It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks and reaches first bloom in roughly 8 weeks. Give it room (12 to 24 in), full sun, and lean soil, go very light on fertilizer, and deadhead or cut flowers to prolong bloom. Leave a few late flowers to drop seed and it returns on its own; wear gloves, since the stems are prickly.

beginner: Borage barely needs feeding and even grows in poor soil. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the ground at planting and that is usually all it needs. Too much fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, just gives you a giant floppy plant with fewer flowers.
seasoned: Borage is a light feeder that thrives even in poor soil, so it needs little supplemental fertilizer. A modest amount of compost or a balanced feed worked in at planting is plenty. Excess nitrogen produces soft, oversized, floppy plants that flower less and are more prone to powdery mildew, so favor a balanced or slightly low-nitrogen feed and skip routine feeding once plants are established.

beginner: It is a good time to give your borage a small feed if you want, but it barely needs it. One light dose of a balanced fertilizer is plenty, and you can skip it if you already added compost.
seasoned: Time for an optional light feed. Borage is a light feeder, so at most one modest dose of a balanced fertilizer supports steady bloom; skip it entirely if your soil already has some fertility or you worked in compost.

beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For borage, a balanced one like 10-10-10 is fine, used sparingly; avoid a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed, which gives leaves instead of flowers.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 worked in lightly at planting suits borage; some growers give a monthly half-strength balanced feed, but a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed only pushes floppy foliage over flowers.

beginner: A little goes a long way. One light feeding at planting is usually enough. If you feed again, use about half what the package says, and do not overdo it.
seasoned: A single light application at planting is usually sufficient; if supplementing, a balanced fertilizer at about half the label rate for annuals is ample. Borage grows well in poor soil, so err toward under-feeding rather than over-feeding.

beginner: Tiny green or black soft insects that can cluster on the tender tips and flower buds, leaving sticky honeydew. Borage is otherwise seldom bothered by pests, and its flowers pull in ladybugs and hoverflies whose young eat aphids, so light infestations often clear on their own. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap handles the rest. Some gardeners even let borage collect aphids as a decoy to keep them off nearby crops.
seasoned: Borage is generally untroubled by insect pests; extension descriptions note it is not usually bothered and has no significant pest problems. When aphids do appear they colonize tender growth and buds, secreting honeydew, but the nectar-rich flowers recruit the aphid predators (ladybugs, hoverflies, lacewings) that keep them in check. Borage is sometimes grown deliberately as an insectary or banker planting for this reason. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap only if populations build.

beginner: A white, powdery film on the leaves, most common in warm, humid, still, or crowded conditions and without enough air movement. It is borage's main disease. Give plants plenty of room, grow them in full sun, water the soil rather than the leaves, and remove badly affected leaves.
seasoned: Borage's signature disease, and essentially its only regular one; it develops in warm, humid, still, and crowded plantings, and worsens as summer heat and humidity build (which is why borage is grown in the cool season in hot climates). Manage culturally with full sun, generous spacing for airflow, base watering, and removal of affected foliage rather than by spraying.

beginner: Borage is drought-tolerant and hates soggy soil. Cold, wet, poorly drained ground can rot its roots and stem base, and young seedlings can collapse at the soil line. Plant in well-drained soil and do not overwater.
seasoned: Borage tolerates dry soil and is intolerant of waterlogging, so the standing failure is root and crown rot (and seedling damping-off) in cold, wet, poorly drained ground. It is a prevention story, not a treatment one: site in well-drained soil, water only when the soil dries, and avoid heavy, water-retentive beds. This is the drought-tolerant plant's usual wet-soil caveat rather than a disease borage is specifically prone to.

beginner: You can keep borage leaves or flowers in the fridge for a day or two, but they wilt fast, so use them right away.
seasoned: Young leaves and freshly picked flowers keep only a day or two loosely covered in the refrigerator and wilt quickly, so use them fresh. Borage does not hold like sturdy produce.

beginner: Borage is a plant for the garden, the bees, and fresh use, not for storing like vegetables. Pick young leaves before they get too fuzzy and prickly, and pick open flowers on a dry day. Snap off the fuzzy green part behind each flower before eating it. The leaves taste like cucumber in salads and drinks, and the blue flowers make a pretty garnish or can be frozen in ice cubes. Only eat borage that has not been sprayed, and eat it only in small amounts: borage leaves contain natural compounds called pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can harm the liver if eaten in large or frequent amounts, so keep borage to a garnish or an occasional few leaves. Wear gloves when you pick it because the stems are prickly.
seasoned: Borage is grown for bloom, a top pollinator draw, and edible leaves and flowers, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply as they would for produce. Harvest young, tender leaves before they turn too bristly, and pick fully open flowers on a dry day; pull off and discard the fuzzy green sepals behind each flower before eating. The leaves taste of cucumber and are used in salads, teas, and cool drinks; the blue flowers are a garnish and can be frozen into ice cubes. Use only unsprayed plants, and eat borage in moderation: the leaves contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which NC State notes can damage the liver and lungs, so use them only sparingly, and borage also has a diuretic effect in large amounts. Wear gloves when harvesting, since the stems and older leaves are prickly.

beginner: The plain blue borage is the classic choice and the best one for bees, and it reseeds itself easily. If you want something different, 'Alba' has white flowers instead of blue, and variegated types like 'Bill Archer' have pretty cream-and-green leaves. They are all the same easy plant with edible flowers and cucumber-tasting leaves, and they all come back from their own dropped seed.
seasoned: For most gardens the ordinary blue species is the one to grow: it is the strongest bee draw, self-sows freely, and gives the classic edible sky-blue stars. 'Alba' is a white-flowered form of the same easygoing plant, useful in white or cottage plantings, and the variegated selections ('Bill Archer', 'Variegata') are grown more for their cream-splashed foliage than for a different flower. All are the same species, are edible-flowered and cucumber-leaved, and come readily from saved or self-sown seed; the simple, open single flowers of every form serve pollinators well.

beginner: Borage is one of the classic companion plants, and its superpower is bees. It flowers for a long time and is a magnet for honey bees, bumble bees, and native bees, so planting it among vegetables draws in pollinators and helpful insects. Gardeners traditionally set it near tomatoes, squash, and strawberries: near squash, melons, and cucumbers it helps pollination; near tomatoes and strawberries it is a long-standing companion said to help them along and bring in the beneficial bugs that eat pests like hornworms. Those pest-fighting claims are garden tradition rather than proven fact, so enjoy borage mainly as a pollinator plant. Just give it lots of room, since it gets big and sprawly, and keep it a bit apart from squash so both get airflow, because they can share powdery mildew.
seasoned: Borage's best-grounded companion value is as a premier insectary and pollinator plant: its long succession of nectar-rich blue flowers strongly attracts honey bees, bumble bees, and native bees, along with beneficial predators, which is well documented by extension. Interplanted around squash, melons, and cucumbers it is credited with improving pollination, and it is a long-standing traditional companion for tomatoes and strawberries (West Virginia University lists it among strawberry companions), with grower lore that it improves their vigor, flavor, and pest resistance and draws in predators of tomato hornworm. Those neighbor-benefit and pest-repellent effects are traditional practice rather than trialed results, so they are framed as tradition. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; site borage for full sun and airflow, give it generous room because it sprawls, and keep it from crowding squash since the two share powdery-mildew susceptibility.

beginner: Borage is one of the very best plants for attracting bees and other pollinators, and it flowers for a long time. An edge or patch of borage brings pollinators and helpful insects to the whole garden.
seasoned: Borage's strongest, best-documented companion function. Its long-blooming, nectar-rich flowers recruit honey bees, bumble bees, native bees, and beneficial predators, supporting pollination and biological control nearby. Plant it as an insectary edge or interplant; this is a habitat and pollination benefit rather than a documented pest-repellent effect.

beginner: Borage's bees help pollinate squash, melons, and cucumbers, which need lots of bee visits to set fruit. Plant borage nearby, but leave room so both get airflow, since they can share powdery mildew.
seasoned: A pollination-support pairing. Cucurbits are bee-pollinated and benefit from more pollinator visits; borage's heavy bee draw makes it a sensible interplant around squash, melons, and cucumbers. Space it generously, since borage and squash share powdery-mildew susceptibility and both want airflow.

beginner: Borage is a traditional companion for tomatoes. Gardeners say it helps tomatoes grow better and brings in insects that eat tomato hornworms. Treat this as helpful garden tradition, and enjoy the bees either way.
seasoned: A classic traditional pairing. Borage is set near tomatoes on the tradition that it improves their growth and disease resistance and recruits predators of tomato hornworm; the mechanism (habitat for beneficials) is plausible but the benefit is traditional practice, not trialed. The dependable payoff is the pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat borage provides.

beginner: Borage is a well-known strawberry companion. Its flowers bring in bees to pollinate the berries, and gardeners plant a few among strawberries to help flavor and yield. Give it room so it does not shade the low strawberry plants.
seasoned: A documented traditional companion for strawberries (West Virginia University lists borage among strawberry companions; UC ANR notes growers tuck a few plants into beds to enhance flavor and yield). The reliable benefit is bee pollination of the berries; keep the large borage plants to the edges so they do not shade the low strawberries.

beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Doing it regularly keeps borage blooming for weeks instead of going to seed, and it also cuts down on how much borage reseeds itself.
